newsitem.title: USA: Dole cuts gap to 5.3 points behind Clinton - poll.
newsitem.headline: Dole cuts gap to 5.3 points behind Clinton - poll.

text.p: Bob Dole jumped to about five percentage points behind President Bill Clinton in the latest Reuters tracking poll on Tuesday, as Republican voters continued "coming home" to their party's candidate.
The poll, conducted for Reuters by John Zogby Group International, produced the best results for Dole in a Reuters survey since its polling began in August.

It showed Clinton at 43.8 percent, Dole at 38.5 percent for a gap of just 5.3 percentage points. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot was at 4.5 percent, 1.9 percent supported other candidates and 11.3 percent were undecided.

"For the first time we have Dole climbing out of the mid-30s. We're getting closer to the election. People are starting to focus, and the Republicans are saying, 'Where do I go?'" pollster John Zogby said in explaining the results.
"Whereas they (the Republicans) were not enthusiastic about Dole, they are coming back to Dole," Zogby said.

The poll was a rolling three day average of results from about 300 interviews a day, Saturday through Monday. The Reuters/Zogby poll of approximately 900 likely voters had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.
Daily tracking polls can show sharp fluctuations due to the relatively small sample of voters polled each day. Their value lies in tracking trend over a period of several days.

Dole's best day was Monday, the day after his first presidential debate with Clinton in Hartford Connecticut. "Factored in with two good days over the weekend, we are now seeing a tight race," Zogby said.

Zogby said that as recently as last week, Dole had been receiving at most 64 percent of Republicans' support. Starting on Saturday, that climbed to the 70 percent range, and by Monday it was 78 percent.

Interestingly, of the voters polled on Monday who had watched the debate, just 13.9 percent thought Dole had won. A much larger 39.8 percent said Clinton was the winner, while 31.8 percent thought it was a tie, and 14.6 percent had no opinion.
Zogby said he found another interesting gap between working mothers and mothers who do not work outside the home.
He said that among white working mothers, Clinton is ahead 46 to 35 percent. But among the white mothers who do not work outside the home, Clinton is ahead by just one point, 41 to 40 percent.
Recalling that the Reuters/Zogby tracking poll showed Clinton ahead by 20 points just last Saturday, Zogby said Dole had narrowed the gap each day since then.

Zogby said he thought Dole had hurt himself last week with his criticism of the Middle East summit Clinton hosted "and that's where Clinton pulled ahead with a big lead. But those sorts of things don't have long leads."

The race for Congress was a dead heat, with 36.7 saying they will vote for the Democratic candidate in their district and 36.8 percent saying they wil vote for the Republican. "As the presidential race tightens, a Republican Congress is more likely," Zogby said.
